newsitem.title: CHINA: Pro-democracy demonstrators test HK streets.
newsitem.headline: Pro-democracy demonstrators test HK streets.

text.p: Thousands of democracy activists marched through central Hong Kong on Tuesday in the first test of the right to protest since China took back the territory from Britain only hours earlier.
The demonstration, which Hong Kong's government-run radio said involved up to 10,000 people, passed off peacefully in a win for all sides.

Beijing-backed authorities were able to point to the march being allowed to go ahead, activists proved they could protest peacefully and Hong Kong's ex-colonial police showed there was no need for Chinese troops to help control internal dissent.
"We want democracy. We want it now," the group chanted. They carried banners reading "Put an end to one party dictatorship" and "Build a democratic China".
They also demanded China reverse the convictions of those who took part in student-led protests in Beijing's Tiananmen Square that were crushed by the military in June 1989.
The march by the Alliance in Support of Democratic Patriotic Movements in China stretched for more than one km (half a mile) through the Central district of Hong Kong.
It included all age groups and there was a smattering of non-Chinese among the protesters.
"We have proved our point that we intend to demonstrate and that we can demonstrate peacefully," an Alliance spokesman said. "This is what democracy is all about, and we will not lose it."

Onlookers enjoying handover national holidays stopped to watch and people packed overhead foot bridges to get a better view of a sight familiar in colonial Hong Kong but in doubt now that China is in charge.
Under the Sino-British agreement that returned Hong Kong to China at midnight on Monday, the territory is to retain many of its civil rights for the next 50 years.
But Hong Kong's new leader, Tung Chee-hwa, has made clear some issue may be off-limits to protests, including personal critcism of China's leaders.
In one change since Tung took over, groups must apply for permits to hold demonstrations rather than simply notifying authorities as in the past.
Anthea Ho, 27, said she was in the protest because she feared democracy would die out in Hong Kong under Chinese rule.
"Hong Kong doesn't have enough democracy now, and if we go backwards, it will be over for us," Ho told Reuters.
Cheung Chi-kwong, 50, a factory-owner, said: "Many pro-democracy supporters are still being persecuted. Why can this happen? We must fight it now."

There was a sizeable police presence but the march turned out to be peaceful and orderly as it wound for two hours through main streets in popular areas like Wanchai and Queensway where there were also many foreign tourists.
Small groups of by-standers joined in, swelling the protest's numbers as it moved along.
After 15 minutes of speeches at the march's destination at the Central Government Offices, the marchers dispersed.
On Monday's handover night, democracy activists had vowed to stage a campaign of protests and called on communist China to hold immediate elections for a new legislature.
